subject: 🤖 AI's Dr. Feelgood?

Plus: Questions for Nvidia | Tuesday, November 10, 2026

Axios Closer
By Nathan Bomey · Nov 10, 2026

Tuesday ✅. Today we're honorary meteorologists, tracking how the winds of AI power are shifting.

🇺🇸 Programming note: We'll be off Wednesday in observance of Veterans Day.

Today's newsletter is 905 words, a 3½-minute read.

📉 The dashboard: The S&P 500 closed down 0.4%.

🥶 Today's stock spotlight: Microsoft (-2.2%) fell after Anthropic debuted several new tools, including Claude Sheets, which could threaten Microsoft Office.

 
 
1 big thing: AI's Dr. Feelgood?
By Pete Gannon
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios. Stock: Getty Images
 

Anthropic shares are set to begin trading next week, just as AI investors are needing a feel-good spark.

  • The AI model developer today said that it will seek to raise up to $62.5 billion in its IPO at a market cap that could top $1 trillion.
  • That's smaller than expected, even when considering that its fully diluted value would grow to $1.4 trillion if stock options are exercised and underwriters buy additional shares.
  • 📈 But that may be just what the doctor ordered — if shares are priced low enough to support a strong secondary showing.

What they're saying: "A successful I.P.O. is arguably required to validate the valuations of stocks in the A.I. ecosystem," Craig Coben, a former top banker at Bank of America, told the New York Times.

🤖 State of play: Nvidia is the closest thing the AI trade has to a single-company proxy.

  • The chip giant's CEO, Jensen Huang, has been the industry's biggest cheerleader and a reassuring voice for investors, with a knack for calming jitters whenever confidence in the AI boom wavers.
  • But now it's Nvidia, and Huang himself, that's causing the jitters. (See below.👇)

🤩 What we're watching: Anthropic's technology has more of a popular wow factor than does Nvidia's sophisticated chips, and it may be able to win over an electorate that has lately been suspicious of AI.

  • And as a public company, Anthropic's fortunes will affect the many Americans who are invested in the stock market through their 401(k)s.

The bottom line: Anthropic is stepping out with a chance to inject some feel-good vibes and reshape the AI market.

Go deeper
 
 
2. 🧐 The $1 trillion man faces serious questions
 

Alice Huang, a suspected spy with whom Jensen Huang admitted having an affair, has reportedly been a top figure at Megaspeed. Photo: Taryn NG/AFP via Getty Images
 

With Nvidia's board and the FBI investigating the Jensen Huang scandal, the company's stock tumbled again today, closing down 5.5% and bringing the market cap to about $4 trillion.

  • Tech bull Dan Ives estimated today that Nvidia would be worth 25%–30% less than it is today without Huang — meaning at least $1 trillion.

Here are several key questions that must be answered:

Did Nvidia give favorable treatment to Megaspeed?

  • If Huang directed a disproportionate amount of chips to Megaspeed — the company led by the suspected spy with whom Huang has admitted having an affair — that's a big problem.

Did he mislead the board?

  • It's one thing if he directed his team to lie to the media. It's a much bigger issue if he lied to the Nvidia board about the relationship.

Did his relationship influence his public position on American chip exports?

  • Huang has been a relentlessly vocal voice in favor of allowing U.S. chips to be sold to China. Did he discuss this with Alice Huang?

When did Nvidia find out that U.S. intelligence officials suspected Alice Huang of being a spy?

  • If it was anytime earlier than a few days ago, was the board doing its fiduciary duty to protect the company or was it focused on protecting the boss?

🗣️ An Nvidia rep had no immediate comment.

⚖️ The latest: Nvidia's board said today that it hired Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct its investigation.

📊 Reality check: Wells Fargo analysts today said they were maintaining their positive outlook on Nvidia shares, despite the key-man risk with Huang, citing the company's leadership position and supply chain capabilities.
 
 
3. 🗞️ The readout
 

GLP-1 drugs, like those seen here, will carry a label warning that they could cause a rare eye condition. Photo illustration: Michael Siluk/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images
 

💉 The FDA will require new language on GLP-1 drugs warning of the potential risk of a rare eye condition. Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk stocks barely moved on the news. (CNBC)

👚 The Children's Place, a kids' clothing retailer, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. It will close an unspecified number of its 495 retail stores in North America. (USA Today)

🚗 Toyota is reviving the Scion nameplate, which it discontinued a decade ago, and plans to make a minicar in Indiana. (Bloomberg)

4. 🕔 After hours: House drones
 

Photo courtesy of Ring
 

Amazon's Ring is rolling out a flying drone and roving robot, letting customers patrol the corners of their homes or businesses whether they're upstairs or out of town, Axios' Nora Eckert writes.

  • Why it matters: Amazon is betting that AI can usher in a new age of autonomous security — with your camera not just watching for trouble, but actively hunting it down.

🚁 How it works: Both the Ring Drone and Rover are powered by AI Pilot, a system that uses cameras, sensors and cloud processing to navigate a home or business autonomously.

  • The drone, which retails for $249.99 and will begin shipping in late January 2027, is designed to fly through corners of your home that a fixed camera can't reach.
  • The roving security device, available for $999.99 starting in mid-December, can roam through businesses on a scheduled pattern or be sent to investigate disturbances.

💭 Nora's thought bubble: As someone who agonizes over whether I turned off the stove, this device sounds intriguing — although I expect my fiery dachshund would have different thoughts about sharing the apartment with a drone.
